title: Can a fruit-fly nervous system learn from financial markets?
author: TenaciousAdvocateD
selftext:
​

I’ve started building a new open-source research project: FlyAlpha.

🔗 GitHub: 

https://github.com/TanaeemDar/FlyAlpha

The idea is simple but unusual:

Use the fruit-fly connectome itself as the neural network.

No Transformers.

No XGBoost.

No conventional policy network.

No backpropagation.

The system will work roughly like this:

Market data → sensory encoding → fly neural activity → LONG / SHORT / FLAT → market outcome → dopamine signal → synaptic learning

The learning system is inspired by the fly’s mushroom body, where dopamine-driven reinforcement can modify neural connections and influence future behavior.

The first goal is not profitability.

The main research question is:

Can a biological neural connectome learn and adapt to a completely foreign environment like financial markets?

I’m building and testing this in stages, including:

• Dopamine ON vs OFF

• Plasticity ON vs frozen

• Real vs randomized connectome

• Random reward

• Resetting learned synapses

The architecture, experiments, failures and results will all remain open source as the project develops.

If you’re interested in connectomics, neuromorphic computing, reinforcement learning or quantitative research, feel free to follow the progress or contribute.

🔗 https://github.com/TanaeemDar/FlyAlpha

FlyAlpha — the fly connectome is the model.

\#OpenSource #ComputationalNeuroscience #Connectomics #NeuromorphicComputing #ReinforcementLearning #QuantResearch

comments.author: DesertClimber
comments.body: Uhhh, you mean like the StonkFly that's already making more on Bitcoin than 90% of regular traders?  LOL

replies.author: TenaciousAdvocateD
replies.body:
Yeah, StonkFly is definitely the closest existing project.

The direction I’m taking FlyAlpha is more experimental: not just “can a fly brain trade?”, but **which parts actually matter for learning?**

I want to test things like degree-preserving connectome randomization, dopamine/plasticity ablations, reward timing, eligibility-window sensitivity, amnesia tests, chronological holdouts, and multi-market validation.

So the goal is less the demo itself, and more isolating whether the fly topology + dopamine plasticity adds measurable out-of-sample learning.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The ablation list is the good part of this. One to add: your randomized connectome should preserve degree distribution and sparsity, not just shuffle edges. Otherwise a real versus random win only tells you structured sparsity beats noise, which is already known and is not a claim about flies.

The harder problem is credit assignment. Dopamine on market outcome gives you one scalar arriving a long way after the decision, and mushroom body plasticity is tuned for reinforcement that lands in seconds. How you bridge that gap will shape the result more than the connectome does.

replies.author: TenaciousAdvocateD
replies.body:
Good point, agreed on both.

For the randomized-connectome control, I should be more explicit that it cannot just be an edge shuffle. The useful control should preserve at least in/out degree distribution, sparsity, synapse-count distribution, and ideally region/type constraints where available. Otherwise the comparison is too easy: biological sparse structure vs broken noise. That would not say anything meaningful about whether fly-specific topology matters.

The credit-assignment issue is also the part I’m most cautious about. A market outcome is a delayed scalar, while mushroom-body dopamine is biologically operating on much shorter behavioral timescales. In the code I’m treating this as a modeling assumption, not a biological claim: eligibility traces bridge the delay, and the dopamine signal is closer to a reinforcement-prediction-error proxy than “profit equals dopamine.”

But you’re right that this mechanism may dominate the result more than the connectome itself. That’s why I think the key controls need to include:

* dopamine disabled
* plasticity frozen
* shuffled connectome preserving degree/sparsity
* randomized reward timing
* varied eligibility-trace decay
* delayed vs immediate reinforcement
* reset-memory / amnesia tests

If performance is only sensitive to the eligibility window and reward timing, then the project has learned something useful, but it would be about the engineered credit-assignment bridge, not about Drosophila topology.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: degree-preserving is the one people skip, and it's the one that matters. a plain edge shuffle destroys so much structure that beating it proves almost nothing.

comments.author: Exciting-World5861
comments.body: pretty cool you should for sure a) create multiple baseline simple systems beforehand to establish the classification/strategy you're attempting because it may well appear to fail simply because of the financial strategy you've chosen eg. long, short, flat is very simplistic classification, because it classifies data of +2% the same as +30%. b) the research question can then not be "can it learn" but "which can it beat" of other established systems eg. threshold, basic ml, xgboost, neural network -> FlyAI !

comments.author: presentofai
comments.body: the connectome evolved to find fruit and mates by smell, so no reason its exact wiring should transfer to price data. the whole thing rides on real-vs-matched-random: if the fly graph beats a degree and sparsity matched shuffle you've got something, otherwise it's a reservoir computer with a good origin story.

replies.author: Gibborish
replies.body: I would imagine that fruit flies are designed to avoid bad smells and go towards good smells, so one could argue they are inherently biased towards bullish trades.

replies.author: presentofai
replies.body: strong case for a long-only fly fund
